World locations & civil clocks

All countries and territories are selectable. Large countries can have several time zones: a country reference point is the default; choose another zone or search a city. Civil clocks use your browser’s IANA time-zone rules. Ancient and far-future legal offsets are not guaranteed.

Click anywhere to set coordinates. Map clicks and typed coordinates retain the selected time zone: choose the correct zone separately. Borders are geographic reference data, not a statement on disputed sovereignty.

Moon & eclipses

Moon sizes and Earth–Moon separation in the main overview are exaggerated when too small to see. Phase diagram is schematic, not a photographic sky orientation.

Search begins at the displayed simulation date, using the selected Earth coordinates.

Educational predictions from Astronomy Engine; weather, terrain and lunar limb effects are not included. Lunar altitude at peak is not a full visibility forecast. Prediction controls support years 1800–2100.

Never look directly at the Sun. Use certified solar-viewing protection; ordinary sunglasses are unsafe.

Gravity calculator: F = G × M × m / (r + h)²

Here r is the radius of the big body and h is how high you are above its surface. Together, r + h is your distance from its centre.

How this matches the real solar system

Real positions. Orbit positions come from NASA/JPL's published Keplerian elements (E. M. Standish and J. G. Williams). Between 1800 and 2050 it uses JPL's high-accuracy table. From 3000 BC to 3000 AD it uses JPL's long-range table, intended for approximate visualization, not precision ephemerides.

Day and night. Each planet's spin axis direction and rotation rate come from the IAU working group values. The page combines the planet's real spin angle with the real direction of the Sun to find where it is noon, where it is night, and where the Sun is straight overhead. For Earth this is accurate to about a minute of time. For other planets the rotation phase is approximate, so it is good for learning but not for exact predictions.

Sunrise on other worlds. A solar day is not the same as one spin. Mercury spins once in 58.6 Earth days but has a 176-day solar day. Venus spins backwards and has a 117-day solar day. Uranus lies on its side, so its poles get decades of continuous daylight and darkness.

Newton mode. Starting from the real positions, only F = G × M × m / (r + h)² between all bodies moves the planets. If the filled planets stay on their rings, Newton's law is reproducing the real motion.

Limits: the main view is a top-down 2D picture of 3D orbits. Earth's position is the Earth-Moon centre of mass. Embedded geographic boundaries and an improved land mask are used and other planets show simple colours and latitude lines. Gas giants have no solid surface, so their rotation is the internal one. Dates before 15 October 1582 use the Julian calendar. Source: NASA JPL Solar System Dynamics.

Sources: NASA/JPL approximate planetary elements; Astronomy Engine (MIT) for Moon and eclipses; Natural Earth geographic data; country presets from mledoze/countries; city search from Open-Meteo/GeoNames. Country reference points are not necessarily capital coordinates. Choose a city preset or search for an exact city.
